headline: Spanish Common Grammar Patterns Foundation
threshold: Use sixty everyday structures, including tener que, hay que, ir a, acabar de and common clause patterns. Ordered for learning, not an asserted statistical frequency ranking.

lessons.title: Tener que + infinitive
lessons.objective: Tener que + infinitive: Conjugate tener for the person; que and the infinitive stay unchanged.

words.es: Tengo que abrir el café a las siete.
words.en: I have to open the café at seven.

words.es: Mi compañera tiene que traer el pan.
words.en: My coworker has to bring the bread.

words.es: Tenemos que preparar las mesas primero.
words.en: We have to prepare the tables first.

words.es: ¿Tienes que salir antes de las diez?
words.en: Do you have to leave before ten?
I do not have to leave today.

words.es: Entonces podemos trabajar juntos hasta el almuerzo.
words.en: Then we can work together until lunch.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing opening a small café. Conjugate tener for the person; que and the infinitive stay unchanged. It expresses a personal obligation. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Hay que + infinitive
lessons.objective: Hay que + infinitive: Hay que expresses a general necessity without naming a subject.

words.en: One needs to arrive with time to spare.

words.es: También hay que traer un cuaderno.
words.en: One also needs to bring a notebook.
Does one have to buy the book today?

words.es: No, pero hay que leer la primera página.
words.en: No, but one has to read the first page.

words.es: Para entrar al aula, hay que mostrar la tarjeta.
words.en: To enter the classroom, one needs to show the card.

words.es: Después hay que guardar silencio durante la explicación.
words.en: Afterward one needs to keep quiet during the explanation.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing before a class begins. Hay que expresses a general necessity without naming a subject. Do not change hay to match the people involved. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Ir a + infinitive
lessons.objective: Ir a + infinitive: Use voy, vas, va, vamos or van plus a and an unchanged infinitive to describe a plan or approaching action.

words.es: Voy a visitar a mi tía el domingo.
words.en: I am going to visit my aunt on Sunday.

words.es: Ella va a preparar el almuerzo.
words.en: She is going to prepare lunch.

words.es: Vamos a llegar antes del mediodía.
words.en: We are going to arrive before noon.
Are you going to bring your children?

words.es: Sí, van a conocer a sus primos.
words.en: Yes, they are going to meet their cousins.

words.es: Después vamos a caminar por el barrio.
words.en: Afterward we are going to walk around the neighborhood.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing planning a short visit. Use voy, vas, va, vamos or van plus a and an unchanged infinitive to describe a plan or approaching action. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Poder + infinitive
lessons.objective: Poder + infinitive: Conjugate poder and keep the second verb in the infinitive.

words.es: Puedo volver a casa en autobús.
words.en: I can return home by bus.
Can you walk with me to the stop?

words.es: Hoy no podemos usar el coche.
words.en: Today we cannot use the car.

words.es: Mi hermana puede llevar las bolsas.
words.en: My sister can carry the bags.
If we finish early, we can walk.
Can we buy the tickets here?

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing finding a way home. Conjugate poder and keep the second verb in the infinitive. It expresses ability, possibility or permission in context. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Querer + infinitive
lessons.objective: Querer + infinitive: Querer plus infinitive keeps the same subject for wanting and doing.

words.es: Quiero aprender a cocinar esta sopa.
words.en: I want to learn to cook this soup.

words.es: Mi hermano quiere mirar la receta.
words.en: My brother wants to look at the recipe.
We want to start after lunch.
Do you want to buy the vegetables with me?

words.es: Sí, pero no quiero salir tan tarde.
words.en: Yes, but I do not want to leave so late.

words.es: Nuestros amigos quieren venir a probarla.
words.en: Our friends want to come and try it.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing choosing an afternoon activity. Querer plus infinitive keeps the same subject for wanting and doing. Compare quiero ir with quiero que vayas, which changes subject and mood. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Necesitar + infinitive
lessons.objective: Necesitar + infinitive: Necesitar followed directly by an infinitive states what the subject needs to do; do not insert que or de.

words.en: I need to check my passport.
I also need to print the reservation.
My friend needs to exchange money.
Do we need to call the hotel?

words.es: No, pero necesitamos confirmar la hora de llegada.
words.en: No, but we need to confirm the arrival time.
Afterward I need to pack the backpack.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing getting ready for a trip. Necesitar followed directly by an infinitive states what the subject needs to do; do not insert que or de. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Deber + infinitive
lessons.objective: Deber + infinitive: Deber + infinitive commonly expresses a duty or recommendation.

words.es: Debes leer la información de la empresa.
words.en: You should read the company's information.
You should also prepare a question.
Should I bring a copy of the document?

words.es: Sí, y deberías llegar diez minutos antes.
words.en: Yes, and you should arrive ten minutes early.

words.es: No debes inventar una respuesta si no sabes.
words.en: You should not invent an answer if you do not know.
We can practice together this afternoon.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing advice before an interview. Deber + infinitive commonly expresses a duty or recommendation. Debes is present; deberías softens advice. Do not confuse deber dinero with obligation. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Gustar + infinitive
lessons.objective: Gustar + infinitive: An infinitive activity acts as a singular subject: me gusta leer.

words.es: Me gusta caminar por la mañana.
words.en: I like walking in the morning.

words.es: A mi hermana le gusta correr.
Nos gusta desayunar juntos los domingos.
words.en: We like having breakfast together on Sundays.
Do you like reading in the park?

words.es: Sí, pero no me gusta llevar muchos libros.
words.en: Yes, but I do not like carrying many books.

words.es: A mis vecinos les gusta escuchar música allí.
words.en: My neighbors like listening to music there.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing talking about free time. An infinitive activity acts as a singular subject: me gusta leer. Me, te, le, nos or les identifies the person who likes the activity. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Me gustaría + infinitive
lessons.objective: Me gustaría + infinitive: Gustaría is conditional and singular before an infinitive.

words.en: I would like to have a coffee.

words.es: A mi amiga le gustaría probar el té.
words.en: My friend would like to try the tea.

words.es: ¿Les gustaría sentarse junto a la ventana?
words.en: Would you like to sit next to the window?

words.es: Sí, nos gustaría ver la plaza.
words.en: Yes, we would like to see the square.

words.es: También me gustaría pedir algo de comer.
words.en: I would also like to order something to eat.

words.es: El camarero nos trae el menú.
words.en: The waiter brings us the menu.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing a polite café order. Gustaría is conditional and singular before an infinitive. Change the experiencer pronoun, not the verb, to say what another person would like. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.

lessons.title: Saber + infinitive
lessons.objective: Saber + infinitive: Saber plus an infinitive means know how to do an activity.

words.en: I know how to prepare a simple presentation.
Ana knows how to draw the plans.

words.es: No sabemos editar el video todavía.
words.en: We do not know how to edit the video yet.
Do you know how to use this program?

words.es: Sí, puedo mostrarles después de clase.
words.en: Yes, I can show you after class.
With practice, we will all know how to do it.

lessons.speaking: You and a Spanish-speaking classmate are discussing sharing skills in a group. Saber plus an infinitive means know how to do an activity. Poder may instead describe current ability or permission. Ask for the missing detail, respond to the partner, clarify one misunderstanding, and agree on the next step. Use examples from the reading and your own details. Explain the grammar in English if asked.
